title: ARE CHRISTIANS REQUIRED TO GIVE MONEY TO THEIR LOCAL CHURCH? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD EXPOSE YOUR HEART—AND SET YOU FREE
paragraphs: ARE CHRISTIANS REQUIRED TO GIVE MONEY TO THEIR LOCAL CHURCH? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD EXPOSE YOUR HEART—AND SET YOU FREE

If God doesn't need your money, why does the Bible speak so seriously about giving? And if Jesus paid for everything at the cross, why are Christians still being told they must give 10%? The answer is more uncomfortable, more beautiful, and more liberating than many churches have ever explained.
There is a moment in church that can make even a faithful Christian uncomfortable.
The worship has been beautiful. The sermon has stirred something deep inside you. You've been reminded that Jesus loves you, that His blood was shed for your sins, and that His grace is sufficient.
Then someone walks to the front and begins talking about money.
Suddenly, something changes.
You remember the electricity bill waiting at home.
The groceries you still need to buy.
The school expenses you haven't figured out.
The medical bills.
The debt.
The salary that seemed enough when you received it but somehow disappeared before the month ended.
And then you hear those familiar words.
"Will a man rob God?"
Your heart sinks.
Because you love Jesus.
You genuinely do.
But you don't know how you're going to make it through another week.
And now you're wondering whether the God who knows your struggles is disappointed because you cannot afford to put money in the offering basket.
Or perhaps you're on the other side of the story.
You've been giving faithfully for years.
You've sacrificed. You've supported your church. You've continued giving even when nobody noticed.
But lately, you've started asking questions you were once afraid to ask.
Is giving 10% actually commanded for Christians under the New Covenant?
Does God consider me disobedient if I give less?
Am I required to give specifically to my local church?
And if I stop giving because I have nothing left, will God stop blessing me?
These are not necessarily questions from a rebellious heart.
Sometimes they come from a wounded heart.
Sometimes from a sincere believer who wants to obey Scripture rather than religious pressure.
And sometimes from someone who has watched money collected in the name of Jesus being handled in ways that look nothing like Jesus.
So let's confront the question without fear.
Not through church tradition.
Not through emotional manipulation.
Not through the promises of prosperity preachers.
And not through the excuses of people who want all the benefits of Christian community without ever contributing to its needs.
Let's go back to Scripture.
Because the truth is this:

The New Testament calls Christians to generous, willing, sacrificial giving, including supporting those who minister to them. But it does not establish a universal requirement that every Christian must give exactly 10% of their income to their local church to remain obedient, blessed, or accepted by God.
And understanding that distinction could change the way you see money, worship, your church, and the heart of Jesus Christ.
Before we go further, remember something.
The One who saved you did not begin His relationship with you by demanding a payment.
He began by giving Himself.
And that changes everything.
In the Old Testament, the practice of tithing was deeply connected to Israel's covenant life.
The Hebrew word commonly translated as "tithe" is מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăśēr), meaning "a tenth."
Under the Mosaic Law, tithes were associated with agricultural produce, livestock, the support of the Levites, religious celebrations, and provision for vulnerable people.
Leviticus 27:30 says:
"And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD's: it is holy unto the LORD."
Numbers 18:21 explains that the Levites received tithes because they had no territorial inheritance like the other tribes of Israel.
Deuteronomy 14:28–29 describes a provision involving the Levites, foreigners, fatherless children, and widows.
This was not simply a modern weekly church collection.
It belonged to a particular covenant arrangement involving Israel's worship, priesthood, land, and communal responsibilities.
And the biblical laws concerning tithes were more complex than the familiar statement, "Everybody must give 10% of their paycheck."
That distinction matters.
Because when we read Scripture faithfully, we must ask not only what a passage says but also to whom it was originally addressed, under which covenant, and how it relates to Jesus Christ.
Consider Malachi 3:8–10.
"Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me."
Those words are real.
They are serious.
And they deserve to be understood rather than ignored.

But Malachi was addressing covenant unfaithfulness among God's people in Israel. The passage speaks of tithes and offerings, the storehouse, and provision in God's house within that historical covenant setting.
It is not automatically a command that every Christian must deposit exactly 10% of a modern salary into a church account.
Nor does the passage give church leaders permission to threaten financially struggling believers with divine punishment.
We cannot faithfully honor Scripture by removing its original context.
And we cannot honor Jesus by turning His Father's Word into a weapon against the vulnerable.
But someone will say, "Didn't Abraham tithe before the Law?"
Yes.
Genesis 14:20 records Abraham giving a tenth of the spoils after his victory.
Hebrews 7 revisits that event in its discussion of Melchizedek and the superiority of Christ's priesthood.
But Hebrews 7 does not command every Christian to give 10% of their regular income to a local congregation.
Its central concern is the greatness of Jesus Christ and His priesthood.
Abraham's action is significant. It demonstrates honor and recognition of God's provision.
Yet describing what Abraham did on that occasion is not the same as establishing a binding percentage for every believer in every generation.
Jacob also promised a tenth in Genesis 28:22, but his vow likewise does not, by itself, establish a universal New Covenant requirement.
Then comes another question.
Didn't Jesus affirm tithing?
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus rebuked religious leaders who carefully tithed small herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He did not praise their hypocrisy.
He exposed it.
His words were spoken to scribes and Pharisees operating within Israel's covenant setting before His death and resurrection.
They show that Jesus did not treat obedience and generosity as substitutes for justice and mercy.
But that passage alone does not settle the question of whether Christians after the resurrection are commanded to give precisely 10% of their income.
And here is where the conversation becomes deeply personal.
Because when Jesus fulfilled the Law and established the New Covenant through His blood, He did not create a people who were less loving, less compassionate, or less generous.
He created a people whose obedience would flow from a transformed heart.
The cross did not make generosity irrelevant.
It gave generosity a new and extraordinary foundation.
Listen to Paul in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
The original Greek is revealing.
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia.
"Each one as he has decided in his heart."
Paul continues:
μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs.
"Not out of grief or under compulsion."
And then:
ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός
Hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
"For God loves a cheerful giver."
The Greek word ἱλαρόν (hilaron) describes cheerfulness or glad willingness.
It does not mean that every offering must be emotionally easy.
Sacrificial generosity can be costly.
Sometimes it comes with tears.
Sometimes it means giving up something you wanted so someone else can receive something they desperately need.
But Paul's point is unmistakable.
Christian giving should not be extracted through coercion.
It should arise from a willing heart responding to God's grace.
And notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, "Every Christian must give exactly 10% or God will withdraw His love."
He does not say, "Your offering determines whether Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for you."
He does not say, "Give money so you can purchase God's favor."
Instead, he points toward willing, thoughtful generosity.
And this is where some people misunderstand grace.
They hear that the New Testament does not impose a universal 10% requirement, and they conclude that giving is unnecessary.
But that is not Paul's teaching either.
Freedom from a fixed percentage is not freedom from love.
Freedom from religious coercion is not permission to become indifferent toward the needs of others.
Grace does not produce a smaller heart.
Grace teaches us to love as we have been loved.
In 2 Corinthians 8:9, Paul writes:
The context is Paul's encouragement of generosity toward believers in need.
And his greatest example is Jesus.
Not a wealthy donor.
Not a successful religious institution.
Not a preacher promising that every offering will return multiplied into your bank account.
Jesus.
The eternal Son of God, who humbled Himself for our salvation.
The Savior who entered human suffering.
The King who wore a crown of thorns.
The Lord who gave Himself on the cross.
Paul grounds Christian generosity in that astonishing grace.
We do not give to make Jesus love us.
We give because, in Christ, we have already encountered a love we could never purchase.
And now consider a woman Jesus noticed when almost everyone else might have overlooked her.
A poor widow.
Mark 12:41–44 tells us that Jesus sat near the temple treasury and watched people putting money into the offering.
Many wealthy people gave large amounts.
Then a poor widow came and put in two small coins.
To the people around her, her gift may have looked insignificant.
But Jesus called His disciples and told them that she had given more than all the others.
Why?
Because the wealthy gave from their abundance, while she gave out of her poverty.
She had given all she had to live on.
Imagine that woman for a moment.
The coins in her hand.
The sound they made when they fell.
The fact that Jesus saw her.
But we must be careful with this passage.
Jesus' recognition of her costly gift is not a command for impoverished Christians to empty their wallets into religious institutions.
In the surrounding context, Jesus condemns religious leaders who "devour widows' houses" (Mark 12:40).
That warning must not be forgotten.
The widow's story should never become an excuse for a church to exploit vulnerable people.
It reveals something precious about the way Jesus sees.
He notices what others overlook.
He knows the difference between abundance and sacrifice.
He sees the heart behind the gift.
And He also condemns religious systems that prey upon the helpless.
That means the struggling single mother who cannot give money this Sunday is not invisible to God.
The unemployed father searching for work is not invisible.
The elderly believer choosing between medicine and an offering is not invisible.
The student surviving on barely enough is not invisible.
And neither is the financially comfortable Christian who has plenty to share but continually finds reasons to keep everything.
Jesus sees both.
He sees poverty.
He sees privilege.
He sees sacrifice.
He sees selfishness.
And He sees what we are afraid to admit about ourselves.
Maybe the real question is not merely, "How much am I required to give?"
Maybe the deeper question is, "What has the grace of Jesus done to my relationship with money?"
Because money has a strange ability to reveal what we trust.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:21:
"For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
Not because money is automatically evil.
Scripture does not teach that.
First Timothy 6:10 identifies the love of money as a root of all kinds of evil, not money itself.
Money can buy food for a hungry family.
It can provide shelter.
It can help a struggling congregation keep its doors open.
It can purchase Bibles for people who have never owned one.
It can fund counseling, relief work, and discipleship.
It can help a pastor devote time to teaching God's Word.
It can also become an idol.
It can feed pride.
It can fund extravagance while the poor are ignored.
It can become a tool of control when religious leaders use fear to obtain it.
The issue is not simply whether money changes hands.
The issue is whether our use of money reflects the character of Christ.
Yes, as a normal expression of Christian generosity and shared responsibility, believers should take seriously the material needs of the congregations and ministries that serve them.
The New Testament provides a real biblical foundation for this.
In Galatians 6:6, Paul writes:
The Greek verb κοινωνείτω (koinōneitō) comes from the family of words associated with sharing and participation.
The verse calls those receiving instruction to share good things with those teaching them.
First Corinthians 9:14 also says:
"Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel."
Paul teaches that gospel workers have a legitimate right to material support, even though he sometimes voluntarily declined that right for the sake of his ministry.
First Timothy 5:17–18 likewise recognizes appropriate honor and material support for elders who labor in preaching and teaching.
These passages matter.
Churches have genuine expenses.
Pastors and ministry workers have genuine needs.
Buildings may require maintenance.
Children need teaching.
The poor need assistance.
Missionaries need support.
Evangelism requires time, effort, and often resources.
Christian communities should not expect faithful ministry to function indefinitely without anyone sharing responsibility.
But notice something equally important.
The same New Testament that teaches support for ministry also teaches accountability, integrity, and care for the vulnerable.
In 2 Corinthians 8:20–21, Paul describes precautions taken in handling a generous collection so that no one could reasonably question its administration.
Financial integrity is not a worldly distraction from ministry.
It is part of faithful stewardship.
A church should not demand trust while refusing reasonable accountability.
A pastor should not be above legitimate questions.
And members should not be shamed for wanting to know how their contributions are being used.
A healthy church should be able to explain its financial priorities with humility and honesty.
Supporting a local church is biblically meaningful.
But financially supporting an institution is not identical to purchasing God's approval.
Nor is every fundraising appeal automatically an expression of God's will.
And giving to a local congregation does not eliminate our responsibility to care for people beyond its walls.
James 1:27 speaks of caring for orphans and widows in their affliction.
First John 3:17 asks how God's love can remain in someone who has material resources, sees a fellow believer in need, and closes their heart.
Galatians 6:10 urges believers to do good to all, especially the household of faith.
Christian generosity is wider than a collection plate.
It includes the hungry neighbor.
The struggling family.
The missionary.
The widow.
The believer facing an emergency.
The person who needs help but cannot repay you.
And sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do with your money is to feed someone who has nothing to eat.
Sometimes it is to help your parents.
Sometimes it is to provide for your children.
First Timothy 5:8 takes responsibility for one's household seriously.
God does not call Christians to use religious giving as an excuse for abandoning legitimate family responsibilities.
That does not mean giving will never require sacrifice.
It means sacrifice must be understood through the whole counsel of Scripture, not isolated emotional appeals.
Paul offers another vital principle in 2 Corinthians 8:12:
"For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."
Read that again.
"According to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."
God is not asking you to pretend you possess resources you do not have.
Paul also explains in 2 Corinthians 8:13 that his purpose is not for others to be eased while the givers are burdened.
His concern is fairness and mutual care.
This is especially important for believers who have been taught that financial hardship proves spiritual failure.
Poverty does not automatically mean someone lacks faith.
Wealth does not automatically prove someone has God's approval.
The cross itself destroys the idea that outward comfort is the measure of divine love.
Jesus was perfectly obedient to the Father.
And yet He suffered.
He was rejected.
He was betrayed.
He was crucified.
If worldly prosperity were the reliable measure of God's pleasure, how would we explain the suffering Savior?
We cannot.
The Gospel is not a transaction in which we hand God money and receive guaranteed financial success.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Forgiveness is received through God's grace, not purchased through offerings.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
Your salvation is not for sale.
Your forgiveness is not for sale.
Your place in God's family is not for sale.
And no preacher, church, or ministry has the authority to put a price tag on what Jesus purchased with His blood.
But here is the other side of that beautiful truth.
When grace truly changes us, we begin asking a different question.
Not, "What is the minimum amount I can give and still be considered obedient?"
But, "Lord, everything I have comes from You. How can I steward it faithfully?"
That question may lead one believer to give 5% of their income during a season of severe financial hardship.
Another may choose 10% as a useful personal discipline.
Another may be able to give 20%, 30%, or considerably more.
These percentages are illustrations of personal decisions, not divinely mandated New Covenant rates.
The amount alone does not establish the spiritual condition of the giver.
A person giving a small amount in love may be making a profound sacrifice.
A wealthy person giving a much larger amount may barely notice the difference.
And neither person should use their giving as a reason to boast.
The Macedonian believers in 2 Corinthians 8 provide a remarkable example.
Despite severe affliction and deep poverty, they overflowed in generosity.
They gave willingly, even beyond what Paul expected.
But what made their generosity extraordinary was not a fundraising technique.
It was their devotion to God.
Second Corinthians 8:5 says they "first gave their own selves to the Lord."
There it is.
The heart of Christian giving.
Before their money, they gave themselves.
And perhaps that is the question Jesus is placing before us today.
Have you given Him your heart?
Not just your Sunday attendance.
Not just your religious vocabulary.
Not just the appearance of Christianity.
Your heart.
Because you can put money into an offering basket while remaining far from God.
You can fund a ministry while refusing to forgive someone.
You can give generously in public while living dishonestly in private.
You can make impressive donations while neglecting your family.
And you can also have almost nothing financially yet possess a heart overflowing with faith, compassion, prayer, and love.
Jesus does not measure spiritual maturity by the size of a bank transfer.
He calls us to follow Him.
To trust Him.
To repent.
To love our neighbors.
To care for the poor.
To live truthfully.
To be faithful with whatever He has entrusted to us.
And yes, to practice generosity.
Not because His grace is incomplete.
But because His grace is powerful enough to transform even the way we handle money.
There is another uncomfortable truth we need to confront.
Some Christians have been deeply hurt by churches that mishandled money.
Perhaps you trusted a leader.
Perhaps you gave when you were struggling.
Perhaps you later discovered that the sacrifices of ordinary members were funding extravagant lifestyles or questionable decisions.
And now every conversation about giving brings back disappointment.
If that is your story, the answer is not to pretend the wrongdoing was acceptable.
Nor is the answer to conclude that Jesus Himself is untrustworthy.
Christ is not the same as every person who claims to represent Him.
He is the Good Shepherd.
He does not exploit His sheep.
He lays down His life for them.
First Peter 5:2–3 instructs church leaders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not by domineering over those entrusted to their care.
That is the biblical standard.
Not intimidation.
Not manipulation.
Not financial secrecy.
Shepherding.
Service.
Integrity.
Love.
If you are in a church where leaders repeatedly threaten you with curses, pressure you to give beyond your means, or refuse reasonable financial accountability, those are serious warning signs.
Seek wise counsel and examine the situation carefully.
You are not dishonoring Jesus by taking His Word seriously.
And if you have become cynical because of what people did in His name, please do not allow their failures to become the final chapter of your faith.
There are faithful churches.
There are humble pastors.
There are believers who serve without applause.
Their work deserves prayer, participation, and, when possible, financial support.
Do not let the misuse of money by some destroy your willingness to practice generosity toward others.
But do not let appeals to generosity silence your responsibility to exercise discernment.
Both truths belong together.
And now we arrive at something that is deeply important to us at Gospel Warrior.
We believe biblical truth should reach beyond church walls.
Beyond geographical borders.
Beyond people who can afford expensive resources.
There are believers hungry for Scripture who cannot purchase every book they need.
There are new Christians who want to understand their faith.
There are struggling people searching for hope late at night.
There are wounded souls who need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Jesus Christ still transforms lives.
Our desire is to help people grow deeper in Jesus Christ through Scripture, discipleship, spiritual encouragement, and resources that point them back to the Gospel.
And we want to continue expanding that work.
Not because you must give money to prove that you love Jesus.
We want to be clear about that because biblical integrity matters more than a persuasive fundraising appeal.
It is an opportunity to participate in a work you value.
These items can be reminders of faith, tools for reflection, and ways to share meaningful Christian messages.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered resources accessible to more people.
You are still welcome here.
You are still valued.
You can still read, learn, grow, pray, and share.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
Think about the people who might see it.
A friend who stopped attending church because someone made them feel ashamed for being poor.
A young believer confused about tithing.
A family member who thinks God is angry because they cannot give 10%.
A Christian who has plenty but has never seriously considered the responsibility of generosity.
A pastor who genuinely wants to teach giving without manipulation.
Or someone who has walked away from faith because religion seemed to care more about their wallet than their soul.
One honest discussion may help someone return to Scripture.
One person may discover that Jesus is not a religious salesman demanding payment for salvation.
He is the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And that is worth sharing.
And I want to ask you something personally.
Not how much you earn.
Not how much you give.
Not what percentage of your income goes to church.
Something deeper.
Have you ever felt guilty, afraid, or spiritually condemned because you could not afford to give money to a church?
Or have you struggled with the opposite problem—knowing that God has blessed you with resources, yet finding it difficult to release your grip on them?
If you have experienced religious pressure around money, you can comment, "I want to give from grace, not fear."
If this article has challenged your own reluctance to be generous, share what God is teaching you.
If you are struggling financially and need prayer, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."
You do not have to reveal private details or disclose your income.
Your honesty may encourage someone who thought they were alone.
Perhaps it will happen tonight.
When the house is quiet.
When your phone is finally put down.
When there is nobody to impress.
Just you and the Lord.
And you ask Him:
"Father, have I been giving because I love You, or because I am afraid of what will happen if I don't?"
"Have I used grace as an excuse to avoid generosity?"
"Have I trusted money more than I have trusted You?"
"Have I ignored someone in need while convincing myself I was being faithful?"
"Have I confused supporting a religious institution with truly following Jesus?"
Those questions may hurt.
But conviction, when it leads us to Christ, is not meant to leave us hopeless.
The Gospel invites us to repentance and restoration.
There is forgiveness for greed.
There is forgiveness for pride.
There is forgiveness for selfishness.
There is healing for those wounded by spiritual manipulation.
There is wisdom for those learning how to give responsibly.
And there is grace for believers who are struggling simply to survive.
You do not need to pretend before Jesus.
He already knows.
He knows the debt.
He knows the anxiety.
He knows the secret fear that there will not be enough.
He knows the generosity nobody applauded.
He knows the selfishness nobody discovered.
He knows the times you wanted to help but couldn't.
And He knows the times you could have helped but chose not to.
Yet His invitation remains.
Come to Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive His grace.
Follow Him in truth.
And allow His love to reshape your life.
Maybe that means beginning to give regularly to your local church, according to your ability, with a willing heart.
Maybe it means increasing your generosity because you recognize that you have been holding back.
Maybe it means asking your church leadership honest questions about financial stewardship.
Maybe it means helping someone whose need is urgent.
Maybe it means making a realistic budget so that your generosity becomes thoughtful and sustainable.
Maybe it means refusing to let fear dictate your giving any longer.
Or maybe, for this season, it means accepting help from the very Christian community you once hoped to support.
Because the church is not supposed to be a place where everyone pretends to have enough.
It is supposed to be a family where people bear one another's burdens.
In Acts 2:44–45, the early believers shared their possessions and provided for those who had need.
Acts 4:34–35 likewise describes resources being distributed according to need.
These passages do not establish a compulsory percentage for every Christian.
They reveal a community profoundly affected by the Gospel.
People were no longer treating their possessions as though they existed only for themselves.
Their faith had become visible through love.

And in Acts 5:4, Peter's words to Ananias confirm that the property and its proceeds were under his control before his deceit. The sin was not failing to surrender a mandatory amount; it was lying to God.
That is a powerful reminder.
God is not impressed by religious appearances.
He desires truth in the inward life.
And if we are going to build ministries in the name of Jesus, they must be built on truth.
Not fear.
Not exaggerated promises.
Not invented biblical obligations.
Not the suggestion that people must pay us to glorify God.

A Christian can glorify God through faithful work, honest business, caring for family, supporting a local congregation, feeding the hungry, praying for others, serving quietly, and sharing the Gospel.
But Jesus must remain greater than the ministry.
Always.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save anyone.
A donation cannot reconcile a sinner to God.
Only Jesus Christ can save.
Only His sacrifice is sufficient.
Only His resurrection gives us the living hope proclaimed in the Gospel.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Are Christians required to give money to their local church?

The most biblically responsible answer is that Christians are called to generous, willing, and responsible financial stewardship, including materially supporting faithful gospel ministry and caring for those in need. The New Testament does not prescribe a universal 10% payment to one's local church as a condition of salvation, God's love, or New Covenant obedience.
A healthy believer should take the needs of their local church seriously.
A healthy church should teach generosity without coercion.
A faithful pastor should handle resources with integrity.
And every Christian should remember that everything we possess is entrusted to us by God.
The goal is not to escape giving.
The goal is to give in a way that honors Jesus.
Because the most remarkable thing about Christianity is not that God asks His people to become generous.
It is that God Himself has already demonstrated generosity beyond anything we could imagine.
Romans 8:32 says:
"He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?"
The Father did not spare His Son.
The Son willingly gave His life.
And the Spirit works within believers to produce new hearts and new desires.
This is the foundation of Christian generosity.
Not a threat from the pulpit.
Not a promise of instant wealth.
Not a desperate attempt to purchase divine approval.
The cross.
The empty tomb.
The grace of God in Jesus Christ.
So when you give, give thoughtfully.
Give prayerfully.
Give willingly.
Give with integrity.
Give in a way that does not neglect the people God has entrusted to your care.
Give without using your generosity to elevate yourself above others.
And when you cannot give money, do not believe the lie that you have nothing meaningful to offer.
You can pray.
You can encourage.
You can serve.
You can share Scripture.
You can visit the lonely.
You can comfort the grieving.
You can help someone carry a burden.
And when God provides you with resources, you can learn to share them faithfully.
Christian generosity is not limited to money.
But neither does it exclude money.
It is the fruit of a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
Jesus did not die to make you a customer of religion.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
He calls you to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
And when His grace takes hold of your heart, even your relationship with money begins to change.
So do not walk away merely asking whether you owe your church 10%.
Walk away asking whether your whole life is being shaped by the One who gave Himself for you.
Because the deepest question was never how much money you could place in God's hands.
It was whether you would place your heart in the hands of Jesus.
And the hands that were pierced to redeem you are not reaching for your wallet to purchase your love—they are calling you to surrender your life.
